newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Author says Tokyo disaster novel based on reality.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Author says Tokyo disaster novel based on reality.

text.p: Japan's worst nightmare comes true. A huge earthquake hits Tokyo in the morning rush hour, killing half a million people as skyscrapers collapse, Tokyo Bay floods and hotels slide into the sea.
Amid searing scenes of death and destruction, the rescue operation is snagged from the start in red tape, while corrupt politicians vie with organised crime and religion to fill the power vacuum.
Alarmist? Fantastic? American writer Albert Alletzhauser insists his book "Quake," describing how the long feared "Big One" razes the Japanese capital, is rooted securely in reality.

"The interesting and perhaps disturbing part of this 'novel' is that many of the characters are based on real people, most of the events are a matter of historical record, while the future events are within the realm of probability," he says in an author's note.

Newspaper reporter Hiroko Fujita is on her way to work when the quake buckles a bridge carrying her commuter train. Alone among the passengers she ignores instructions to wait patiently for help that never comes, and scrambles to safety just before the train and its occupants plunge to their deaths.

Fujita's odyssey in search of her son is transmitted live to the outside world via her mobile phone, a search which introduces the reader to a cast of characters including a corrupt government minister, a crime boss and a dissolute American finance trader.

In "Quake", Alletzhauser's second book, he uses a fictional framework to tell a graphic story of horror and romance but which draws uncomfortable conclusions about contemporary Japanese life, particularly the alleged lack of earthquake-proof buildings and general disaster preparedness.
"There are nine million buildings in Tokyo. Seven million are made of wood. When, not if, the Big One hits, they'll go up in flames," Alletzhauser told Reuters.
AUTHORITIES UNPREPARED

In a final chapter he wrote: "Chaos will reign when the Big One hits, with lines of authority crossed in both Tokyo and national government. Every government organization lives in its own little earthquake fantasy world with separate budgets, communications systems, seismograph stations and preparedness plans. There is no central authority."

Alletzhauser visited Kobe shortly after the January 17, 1995 quake, Japan's worst natural disaster for more than 70 years in which 6,336 people were killed and 34,900 injured. Authorities estimate at 9.9 trillion yen ($80 billion) the financial damage of the quake, which measured 7.2 on the Richter scale.

Now living in South Africa, Alletzhauser said he learned first-hand from the Kobe mayor's office about systematic looting by crime gangs, and grisly details of the kind of injuries which an earthquake produces.
"There was a pattern between the Kobe quake and those in 1906 in San Francisco and 1923 in Tokyo in the large numbers of people who had to have trapped limbs amputated," he said.
A newer menace was posed by shards from the glass tops of office desks "hurtling horizontally at 200 miles an hour," he said.
HOPING FOR MOVIE VERSION
Alletzhauser said he would negotiate film rights for "Quake" and categorised it alongside the disaster movies "Twister" and "Independence Day" but with one important difference.

"This was a new type of genre that I was coming up with, it's a docu-drama, a thriller, where the reader can read it but they learn something, they know intense research has gone into it," Alletzhauser said.
He was anxious to nail what he called one misconception in Western capitals -- that a severe earthquake would wipe out the value of the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE).

"This is not the case. The TSE is simply a place where buyers meet sellers. All records are kept by stockbrokers and all stock certificates by clients, stockbrokers, the Japanese Securities Agents, or the Japan Securities Deposit Centre in Kayabacho," Alletzhauser wrote.

As a financial centre, "Tokyo is totally out of sync with the rest of the world. Tokyo's in the middle of a massive bear market, everybody's depressed, the rest of the world is booming. We cannot say that if Tokyo goes down in the future the rest of the world will go down, but there will be ramifications."
MARKETS MIGHT FIND SILVER LINING

Like some unscrupulous traders in Quake, "people would sickly, perversely see it as an opportunity to buy a marker which has traditionally been firm," Alletzhauser said of the likely impact of a Tokyo earthquake on world financial markets.

Tokyo stocks fell one percent after publication of Alletzhauser's "The House of Nomura" -- a non-fiction book about the Japanese securities house. Nomura sued him for libel in London, but later withdrew the lawsuit.

Japan is one of the world's most active seismic hotspots and many Tokyo residents live in fear of the "Big One," a seemingly overdue killer quake. An earthquake centred offshore, measuring 6.6 on the Richter scale, shook the Tokyo area on September 11, 1996, but caused no noticeable damage.
Politicians are taking no chances.

"It is incumbent on Japan to learn the lessons of the (1995) earthquake and construct a broad-ranging disaster relief policy to put at ease people worried the same thing can happen again," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on the first anniversary of the disastrous Kobe quake. ($ = 122.3 Japanese Yen)
